title: Trident Financial Services x Redwood — Procurement / Legal (DPA + SLA + Residency)
summary: Procurement/legal working session to align Redwood Dedicated vs Private commercial terms. Trident requested US-only data residency, tighter audit/retention language, and clarified roles (processor/sub-processor). They proposed lower liability cap and broader indemnities; Redwood flagged standard positions and agreed to provide written counter language. SLA credit structure, support response times, and a DPA exhibit for subprocessors were discussed. Follow-ups include counsel review of DPA redlines, residency/retention exhibit, and confirming whether the deal will run via AWS Marketplace private offer.
topics: Commercial structure (Dedicated vs Private; Marketplace private offer)
DPA: roles, data use, retention, subprocessors, breach notification
Security: SOC 2 report access, audit logs, encryption/KMS responsibilities
Data residency: US-only processing + log storage; disaster recovery region
SLA: uptime definition, service credits, support response times
Liability cap, excluded damages, and indemnity scope
Order form exhibits and procurement timeline
action_items: Michael Grant (Redwood) — Send DPA redline package + Redwood proposed fallback language for residency/retention — Due 2025-06-06
Sofia Mendes (Redwood) — Share SLA v2 (Dedicated/Private) with service credit table + definitions (availability window, exclusions) — Due 2025-06-06
Priyom Das (Redwood) — Confirm commercial path: direct order form vs AWS Marketplace private offer; send quote reflecting preferred path — Due 2025-06-07
Monica Shah (Trident) — Confirm Trident’s required breach notification window and whether 72 hours is acceptable — Due 2025-06-07
Derek Liu (Trident) — Review Redwood liability/indemnity counters; propose acceptable cap and IP indemnity carveouts — Due 2025-06-10
Ravi Menon (Trident) — Validate DR / secondary region requirements for Private (US-only) and whether dual-region is mandatory — Due 2025-06-10
next_steps: Redwood to send consolidated redlines + exhibits (DPA/SLA/subprocessor list/residency addendum).
Trident legal to return proposed liability cap + indemnity edits.
If Marketplace: align on AWS private offer paperwork + required fields; otherwise proceed with order form signature route.
Schedule 30-min follow-up early next week to close open terms and confirm signature timeline.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai meeting transcript

Title: Trident Financial Services x Redwood — Procurement / Legal (DPA + SLA + Residency)
Date/Time: Jun 5, 2025 2:03 PM ET
Duration: 52 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Priyom Das, Michael Grant, Sofia Mendes
Trident Financial Services: Elaine Porter (Procurement), Derek Liu (Legal), Monica Shah (Vendor Risk), Ravi Menon (Platform Eng)

---
Summary (auto)
- Reviewed DPA redlines: data residency, retention, sub-processors, breach notification.
- Reviewed SLA terms: availability, credits, support response times.
- Discussed liability cap and indemnities; agreed to exchange written counter-proposals.

Action items (auto)
- Redwood to send updated DPA/SLA exhibits and subprocessor list.
- Trident to confirm breach notice window and DR region requirements.
- Schedule follow-up for next week.

---

[00:00] Priyom Das: Alright, cool. Thanks everyone for making time. Goal today is basically to go through the redlines on the DPA and the SLA, and then make sure we’re aligned on the residency and the liability stuff. Michael and Sofia are here from our side.

[00:18] Elaine Porter: Thanks Priyom. Yeah, we want to get this to a signature-ready state. We’re trying to keep momentum because the pilot went well, but the redlines are… a few.

[00:30] Derek Liu: (laughs) A few is accurate.

[00:32] Sofia Mendes: Understood.

[00:35] Priyom Das: Maybe quick round of context. Ravi, I know you’re the technical owner. Are you still expecting Private in our VPC, or are we doing Dedicated hosted?

[00:45] Ravi Menon: We’re leaning Private in our AWS account, VPC. Dedicated could work but our security team keeps circling on network boundaries and residency. We can do a private offer through Marketplace if that helps procurement.

[01:03] Elaine Porter: Marketplace would help. Not mandatory, but it helps.

[01:07] Priyom Das: Got it.

[01:08] Michael Grant: From legal’s side, just note that Marketplace changes who signs what, but the DPA and data terms still matter.

[01:16] Derek Liu: Right, we still require a DPA and a security addendum even through Marketplace.

[01:23] Priyom Das: Makes sense.

[01:25] Michael Grant: Okay, I’m looking at your redline doc. First big bucket: data residency. You’ve added a requirement that “all Customer Data, including telemetry and derived data” stays in the United States, and that support access is US persons only. Can you clarify the intent there?

[01:44] Monica Shah: Sure. For our regulated workloads, we can’t have processing outside the US. And our policy language includes logs. Sometimes vendors say “we only process prompts in region” but then logs go to like, Ireland, or a global logging bucket.

[02:00] Ravi Menon: Also, we had an issue with another provider—Azure OpenAI—where a support escalation ended up involving a team outside the US. So we want to make it explicit.

[02:13] Michael Grant: Understood. For Private deployments, if this is in your AWS account, the compute and the storage are in your control, so the residency requirement is mostly satisfied by architecture. For Redwood-managed components—like optional control plane services—we can commit to US region hosting. We can’t generally commit to “US persons only” without defining it, but we can commit to access controls, least privilege, and that support access is limited to authorized personnel. We can discuss a geo restriction.

[02:42] Derek Liu: We can draft it as “support personnel located in the US” rather than citizenship. That’s fine.

[02:49] Sofia Mendes: Also we should align what “Customer Data” includes. Your redline includes “derived data.” We typically exclude aggregated, anonymized telemetry used to operate the service.

[03:01] Derek Liu: If it’s truly anonymized and can’t be re-identified, fine. But we don’t want prompts or completions used for training, and we don’t want them leaving the region.

[03:13] Priyom Das: Just to be explicit: Redwood doesn’t use customer prompts for training by default. For Private, it’s in your boundary anyway.

[03:22] Monica Shah: Okay, but we need it in writing.

[03:25] Michael Grant: Yep. We have standard language: “Customer Content not used to train.” I’ll make sure the DPA states it clearly.

[03:33] Ravi Menon: On logs: we need audit logs and operational logs. Some can contain request IDs, maybe model name, token counts, but not raw prompts ideally.

[03:45] Priyom Das: Right. Our audit logs are configurable. We can avoid logging prompt text by default; there are fields like timestamp, actor, endpoint, model, response status, tokens, and then you can integrate export.

[03:59] Ravi Menon: Okay. So we can say “logs do not contain prompt or completion content by default.” That would help.

[04:08] Michael Grant: We can put that in a security exhibit rather than DPA, but yes.

[04:14] Derek Liu: A security exhibit is fine as long as it’s contractually binding.

[04:18] Sofia Mendes: It can be an exhibit to the order form.

[04:22] Priyom Das: Next point is retention. Derek, you had 0-day retention language for all content plus a 7-day cap for logs.

[04:32] Derek Liu: Correct. Our baseline is that vendors should not retain content, and logs should be minimal. We can make exceptions for security investigation, but we want it bounded.

[04:45] Priyom Das: For Private deployments, content retention is up to your storage policy. Redwood doesn’t need to store prompts at rest. For Redwood-managed operational logs—if we’re running any part—we typically retain for 30 days. Seven might be tight operationally.

[05:03] Monica Shah: Our policy says 30 is acceptable if we can configure it and if it’s US-only.

[05:11] Sofia Mendes: Okay so maybe the path is: content retention “none” by default, and operational logs 30 days default, configurable down to 7 with request?

[05:23] Ravi Menon: I’d prefer it configurable. We might keep audit logs longer on our side for SOX.

[05:29] Priyom Das: That matches: you export audit logs to your SIEM, keep them whatever you want.

[05:36] Michael Grant: I’ll propose language: “Redwood retains operational logs for up to 30 days unless otherwise configured” and “Customer may export audit logs.”

[05:47] Derek Liu: Okay.

[05:49] Michael Grant: Subprocessors. You asked for 30 days prior notice for any new subprocessors and the right to terminate if you object.

[05:58] Derek Liu: Standard for us.

[06:00] Michael Grant: We can do notice and an objection process. The right to terminate is usually limited to the affected service if we can’t resolve. We can align.

[06:12] Monica Shah: Also we need the list. The current doc says “available upon request.” Procurement needs it attached.

[06:18] Sofia Mendes: We can provide the current list as an exhibit. For Private deployments, subprocessors are limited—mostly support tooling, ticketing, and maybe monitoring if enabled.

[06:30] Priyom Das: We’ll send the list.

[06:33] Derek Liu: Breach notice. We put 48 hours.

[06:36] Michael Grant: We generally do “without undue delay” and then a target like 72 hours after confirmation. 48 is hard because sometimes you don’t know what happened in 48.

[06:51] Monica Shah: Our internal policy is 72. Legal asked 48 as a negotiation opener, honestly.

[06:58] Derek Liu: (overlap) Yeah, 72 is probably fine as long as it’s “after confirmation” and you do an initial notice quickly.

[07:06] Michael Grant: Great. We can do: initial notification without undue delay, and then details within 72 hours of confirming a breach.

[07:16] Priyom Das: SLA. Sofia, do you want to run that section?

[07:20] Sofia Mendes: Sure. Trident proposed 99.99% uptime with no exclusions and credits starting at 99.9. Our standard for Dedicated is 99.9 monthly availability, with standard exclusions like planned maintenance and customer-caused outages. For Private, availability is somewhat shared responsibility because it’s in your VPC/AWS account.

[07:43] Ravi Menon: That’s a big point. We want Redwood to own the app layer, but we’re owning AWS infra.

[07:50] Sofia Mendes: Exactly. So we can provide an SLA on the Redwood software service components we manage, but not on your AWS outages.

[07:58] Derek Liu: Can we define the “Service” precisely and tie availability to the control plane and the inference endpoint? Like, if your inference service is up but your auth service is down, that’s still an outage.

[08:12] Sofia Mendes: Yes, we can define service components. The credits: you proposed 25% monthly fee credit at 99.9 and 50% below 99.0. Our standard is lower. We can counter with a tiered structure.

[08:29] Elaine Porter: Honestly, credits matter less than the commitment and the clarity. We just need something procurement can live with.

[08:37] Priyom Das: And practically, the architecture includes fallback policies, so app-level uptime can be higher.

[08:45] Ravi Menon: If we do multi-region, maybe. But residency says US only, and even within US we need to know if DR is single-region or dual.

[08:58] Priyom Das: Good call. We can do dual region within US—like us-east-1 and us-west-2—depending on the deployment plan and cost. But we need to confirm if you require it for production.

[09:10] Ravi Menon: I’ll take that back. I’m not sure if our policy requires dual region for this specific workload.

[09:16] Monica Shah: Vendor risk may, depending on criticality.

[09:20] Sofia Mendes: Okay. On support response times, you asked for P1 within 1 hour 24/7. We can do that on our enterprise support tier. That would be part of the Private package.

[09:32] Elaine Porter: Great.

[09:34] Derek Liu: Liability cap. This is the bigger issue. Your standard cap is 12 months fees. We typically do 2x fees, but we also require uncapped for confidentiality and security breach.

[09:50] Michael Grant: We can’t do uncapped for security incidents. The market standard is either 12 months fees or a higher cap for data security, but not uncapped.

[10:02] Derek Liu: We can consider a separate cap for security breach.

[10:06] Sofia Mendes: What are you thinking? Like 2x annual fees for security, 1x for everything else?

[10:12] Derek Liu: Something along those lines. Also, your limitation of liability excludes “loss of data” entirely. That’s not workable if the claim is data loss.

[10:25] Michael Grant: We exclude consequential damages. “Loss of data” sometimes gets interpreted as consequential. We can clarify that direct costs of restoring data aren’t excluded, while lost profits are excluded.

[10:41] Derek Liu: That’s helpful.

[10:43] Priyom Das: From our side, we’d like to keep it consistent and avoid weird edge cases. But we understand regulated buyers.

[10:52] Derek Liu: Indemnities: you have IP infringement indemnity; we want it to cover third-party claims that the service violates law, plus a broader data breach indemnity.

[11:06] Michael Grant: We can do standard IP indemnity. “Violates law” is very broad. For data breach, we can do commitments around security measures and incident response, but indemnity is tricky.

[11:20] Monica Shah: Our risk team typically asks for indemnity or at least specific remedies.

[11:26] Sofia Mendes: Remedies could be service credits plus termination rights, and we can discuss insurance certificates.

[11:34] Elaine Porter: Yes, can you provide your cyber insurance certificate?

[11:38] Michael Grant: We can provide a certificate of insurance.

[11:40] Priyom Das: Also SOC 2.

[11:42] Monica Shah: SOC 2 Type II, yes. We need the report under NDA.

[11:47] Michael Grant: We can share it under NDA via our evidence pack process. I’ll send the request steps.

[11:55] Derek Liu: Okay.

[12:01] Priyom Das: Switching gears: data residency again—your redline says “no cross-border remote admin access.” In practice, our support team is distributed. But for Private, we can restrict who has access and route support through your bastion. Would that work?

[12:20] Ravi Menon: If access is through our systems and we approve it, yes. We can also require just-in-time access and session logging.

[12:30] Priyom Das: We support JIT access patterns. We also have audit logs of admin actions.

[12:36] Monica Shah: We’ll need that stated.

[12:39] Michael Grant: We can incorporate it in the security exhibit: access requires customer authorization, session logging, and all admin actions are auditable.

[12:49] Derek Liu: Good.

[12:52] Sofia Mendes: On commercial paperwork: if we do AWS Marketplace private offer, the SLA sometimes is tied into the private offer terms. But we can attach our SLA exhibit and DPA.

[13:05] Elaine Porter: Marketplace is preferred. Our AP process is faster.

[13:10] Priyom Das: OK, I’ll confirm with partnerships, but we’ve done private offers. There’s a template.

[13:18] Ravi Menon: If it’s Marketplace, does that change data processing? Like, is AWS a subprocessor in that case?

[13:26] Michael Grant: AWS is already a subprocessor for cloud infrastructure if we run anything in AWS. In Private in your account, you are contracting with AWS separately. But for any Redwood-managed services, AWS is a subprocessor. We can clarify roles.

[13:43] Derek Liu: Also, please clarify if Redwood is a processor or subprocessor. For our customer data, you’re a processor, we’re controller.

[13:51] Michael Grant: Yes, we’ll state that. We’re processor with respect to customer personal data we process for the service.

[14:00] Priyom Das: Quick note: a lot of the “personal data” may not even be involved if you’re not sending PII/PHI, but we’ll treat it as if it might.

[14:09] Monica Shah: We will treat it as potential NPI. So yes.

[14:15] (crosstalk) 

[14:16] Sofia Mendes: One thing on pricing: not for today, but we’ll need to ensure the order form references the correct support tier and uptime target. Elaine, do you need a revised quote with Marketplace language?

[14:28] Elaine Porter: Yes, with the private offer, and please show the term length and any annual commit. Our finance team wants clarity.

[14:37] Priyom Das: Will do.

[14:40] Derek Liu: Back to the DPA. There’s a clause about you being able to change security measures unilaterally. We need notice and no material reduction.

[14:50] Michael Grant: That’s reasonable. We can add: no material reduction, and we’ll provide notice for material changes.

[14:59] Monica Shah: Also audit rights. We require ability to audit.

[15:03] Michael Grant: We can provide third-party audit reports—SOC 2—rather than on-site audits, unless required by law. On-site audits are hard at scale.

[15:14] Derek Liu: That’s fine. We can frame audit as report-based, with a right to request additional info.

[15:22] Ravi Menon: For the POC we got sample audit logs. Can we reference that schema in docs?

[15:28] Priyom Das: Yep. We have an audit log schema doc we can share; it includes fields and export options.

[15:36] Monica Shah: Great.

[15:38] Sofia Mendes: Service credits. Derek, do you need credits payable as refund or just credit against next invoice?

[15:45] Derek Liu: Credit against fees is fine.

[15:48] Elaine Porter: Yeah, that’s standard.

[15:51] Sofia Mendes: Okay.

[15:53] Priyom Das: Can I ask—what are you comparing us against? Just to understand pressure points.

[16:00] Ravi Menon: Bedrock and Vertex. Bedrock is easy procurement-wise, but performance and control are not great. Together is another one for “VPC-ish” but less enterprise process.

[16:14] Priyom Das: Got it.

[16:16] Derek Liu: And those big clouds give us better liability positions sometimes, which is why we’re pushing.

[16:24] Michael Grant: Understood. We’ll offer a reasonable compromise but we need to keep it within our risk tolerance.

[16:31] Monica Shah: Another thing: data deletion. Your DPA says 90 days after termination. We need 30.

[16:40] Michael Grant: For Private, data deletion is in your control. For any Redwood-held data, we can do 30 days. We just need to ensure backups are handled.

[16:50] Derek Liu: Backups can be 90 if it’s inaccessible and then deleted on a rolling basis. But state it.

[16:58] Michael Grant: Okay.

[17:01] Priyom Das: Let’s talk timeline. Elaine, what’s your target signature date?

[17:06] Elaine Porter: End of month is ideal. Realistically, we need legal alignment next week to stay on track.

[17:13] Priyom Das: So we should aim to send you our consolidated response by tomorrow.

[17:18] Michael Grant: Yes.

[17:19] Sofia Mendes: Works.

[17:22] Derek Liu: Please send it as a single redline, not 10 PDFs.

[17:26] Michael Grant: (laughs) Noted.

[17:28] Priyom Das: A couple more technical-legal intersections. Monica, you asked whether prompts/completions ever leave the VPC for “optimization.” The answer is no, not without explicit enablement. But we should phrase that carefully.

[17:43] Monica Shah: Yes, we’ve seen vendors say “we don’t train” but then they do “service improvement.” We want “no training, no improvement” unless opted in.

[17:52] Michael Grant: We can add an explicit opt-in for any use beyond providing the service.

[17:58] Derek Liu: Good.

[18:00] Sofia Mendes: Also confidentiality: your edits add “confidentiality obligations survive indefinitely.” We typically do 5 years, but for trade secrets it’s longer.

[18:10] Derek Liu: We can accept 5 years with trade secrets indefinite.

[18:14] Sofia Mendes: Great.

[18:18] (brief silence)

[18:20] Priyom Das: Any other open items we should address live?

[18:23] Ravi Menon: The definition of “availability.” We need it to include auth, not just inference. Also, maintenance windows should be outside business hours.

[18:33] Sofia Mendes: We can define availability for “API endpoint + auth” collectively. Maintenance windows: we can provide notice and schedule off-hours, but sometimes urgent patches happen.

[18:45] Derek Liu: Put urgent patches as exception with notice as feasible.

[18:49] Sofia Mendes: Okay.

[18:52] Monica Shah: And incident response: you have 10 business days to provide post-mortem. We need 5.

[19:00] Michael Grant: Five business days is aggressive but we can commit to an initial RCA within five and a final within 10.

[19:09] Monica Shah: That works.

[19:12] Elaine Porter: One more procurement thing: payment terms. Standard is Net 45. Your order form says Net 30.

[19:19] Sofia Mendes: We can do Net 45 for enterprise customers.

[19:23] Elaine Porter: Great.

[19:25] Priyom Das: Cool.

[19:27] Derek Liu: So next is you send us your counter. We’ll review internally, and then we schedule a follow-up?

[19:34] Priyom Das: Yes. I propose we do Tuesday, 30 minutes.

[19:38] Elaine Porter: Tuesday 2 PM ET works.

[19:41] Priyom Das: Great.

[19:43] Michael Grant: Just to recap what we’re sending: updated DPA with residency/retention language, subprocessor exhibit, breach notice language, deletion language; and then SLA with definitions and credit table.

[19:58] Sofia Mendes: And a note on Marketplace private offer vs direct order form.

[20:03] Priyom Das: Plus SOC 2 access steps and insurance cert.

[20:07] Monica Shah: Perfect.

[20:09] Derek Liu: And we’ll respond with a proposal for the liability cap structure and any indemnity changes we still need.

[20:16] Priyom Das: Sounds good.

[20:18] (Transcript continues with detailed clause-by-clause discussion; some minor sections omitted by Fireflies)

[21:02] Derek Liu: On the cap, if we can land on 2x annual fees for security and confidentiality, and 1x for everything else, that likely clears.

[21:12] Michael Grant: I can’t commit on the call, but we’ll consider and propose.

[21:17] Sofia Mendes: We’ll run it through our approvals.

[21:20] Priyom Das: Okay.

[22:05] Ravi Menon: Also can you state “no customer content stored in training datasets” explicitly.

[22:10] Michael Grant: Yes.

[23:44] Monica Shah: For the subprocessor notice, 30 days is minimum.

[23:49] Michael Grant: We can do 30 days.

[25:30] Elaine Porter: For Marketplace, we’ll need vendor onboarding info—tax forms, etc.

[25:36] Priyom Das: We have it. I’ll send.

[27:12] Derek Liu: Your DPA references GDPR SCCs. Do we need SCCs if US-only?

[27:18] Michael Grant: If there’s no transfer, SCCs shouldn’t apply. We can leave them as optional module.

[27:28] Derek Liu: Okay.

[29:40] Sofia Mendes: On termination for convenience, you asked for 30 days. We typically do no termination for convenience on annual commits.

[29:49] Elaine Porter: That’s fine. We can keep standard.

[31:05] Monica Shah: Do you have a right to use our name/logo?

[31:09] Sofia Mendes: No, only with permission.

[31:12] Derek Liu: Put that in the MSA.

[31:15] Michael Grant: Will do.

[34:22] Ravi Menon: For Private, does Redwood have any telemetry leaving our VPC?

[34:28] Priyom Das: Optional. We can configure it to stay local, and you can disable outbound egress. We’ll document required endpoints if any.

[34:40] Monica Shah: Great.

[36:58] Derek Liu: Any arbitration clause?

[37:01] Michael Grant: Standard venue clause; we can discuss arbitration if needed, but usually not.

[39:15] Elaine Porter: Okay, I think we have enough.

[39:18] Priyom Das: Great. Anything else before we close?

[39:22] Derek Liu: No, just send the consolidated package.

[39:25] Monica Shah: And the SOC 2 steps.

[39:27] Priyom Das: Yep.

[39:29] Priyom Das: Thanks everyone.

[39:31] Meeting ended.

---
Notes
- Some portions are marked as “omitted” due to cross-talk and screen-share reading of contract language.
- Terms discussed are non-binding until finalized in writing.
